Question: Silver chloride, a white solid that barely dissolves in water, vanishes when the stockroom worker pours in concentrated ammonia. A silver-ion electrode in the clear solution reads almost nothing. Where did the silver go, and what holds it?
Answer: NH₃ (Lewis base, lone pair) binds Ag⁺ (Lewis acid): Ag⁺ + 2NH₃ ⇌ Ag(NH₃)₂⁺, Kf 1.7 × 10⁷ (OpenStax 15.2). Free Ag⁺ falls far below what AgCl's Ksp allows, so AgCl keeps dissolving (coupled equilibria). With ammonia in excess, free [Ag⁺] = Kd [complex] ÷ [NH₃]², millions of times less than the silver present.
Target concept: A ligand that binds a metal ion strongly leaves almost no free metal ion; with the ligand in excess, x = Kd C ÷ Lⁿ.

Question: Black-and-white film is developed, then soaked in a fixer bath of sodium thiosulfate, which dissolves the leftover silver bromide so the picture stops darkening in light. A silver-ion electrode in used fixer reads almost no free silver ion. Which species holds the silver, and why is so little free silver left?
Answer: S₂O₃²⁻ binds Ag⁺: Ag⁺ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ ⇌ Ag(S₂O₃)₂³⁻, Kf 4.7 × 10¹³ (OpenStax 15.3, Example 15.16). With thiosulfate in excess, nearly all silver is complexed; free [Ag⁺] = Kd [complex] ÷ [S₂O₃²⁻]², about 10¹¹ to 10¹³ times less than the silver present.
Target concept: With a very large Kf and the ligand in excess, the free metal ion is x = Kd C ÷ Lⁿ, tiny next to the metal present.

Question: Pale blue copper(II) sulfate solution turns a deep, inky blue when plenty of ammonia is added. A colorimeter set to the deep blue reads high, while a copper-ion electrode reads almost nothing. Which species makes the deep blue, and how many ammonia molecules does each copper ion hold?
Answer: Cu²⁺ + 4NH₃ ⇌ Cu(NH₃)₄²⁺ (deep blue), Kf 1.7 × 10¹³ (Appendix K). Four NH₃ lone pairs bind each Cu²⁺. With ammonia in excess, free [Cu²⁺] = Kd [complex] ÷ [NH₃]⁴: about 10¹¹ to 10¹³ times less than the copper present.
Target concept: When n ligands bind, the ligand concentration is raised to the nth power in Kf and Kd.

Question: Aluminum hydroxide, the white paste in some antacids, does not dissolve in water, yet it dissolves in strong sodium hydroxide solution. A test on the clear result finds no free aluminum ion at all. Which species holds the aluminum, and why is the free ion so scarce?
Answer: Al(OH)₃ is amphoteric. In excess OH⁻: Al³⁺ + 4OH⁻ ⇌ Al(OH)₄⁻, Kf 1.1 × 10³³ (OpenStax 15.3). Free [Al³⁺] = Kd [complex] ÷ [OH⁻]⁴ ≈ 10⁻³⁴ M: far less than one ion in any real volume, so effectively none.
Target concept: An enormous Kf with the ligand in excess leaves a free metal concentration so small that it means no free ions at all.
